analysis.one_liner: Caps federal student loan interest rates at 4-6%, kills origination fees, and lets older borrowers refinance.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee on July 10, 2017 and never received a hearing, vote, or any cosponsors before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lower the interest rate caps on new federal student loans to 4% for undergraduates, 5% for graduate students, and 6% for parents borrowing for their children. It would also stop charging students an origination fee — a fee of roughly 1% taken out of every loan before the student even receives it — and create a program letting people with older federal loans, including older bank-issued federal loans, refinance them at the new lower rates. The refinancing program would prioritize borrowers with the greatest financial need, based on income rules the Education Secretary would write.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future federal student loan borrowers. Students taking out new loans after July 1, 2018 would face lower interest caps (4% undergraduate, 5% graduate, 6% for parent PLUS loans), keep more of their loan money because the origination fee disappears, and borrowers with older federal loans could refinance down to the rates offered to new borrowers, which would lower their monthly payments and total interest paid over the life of the loan.

how_it_helps.text: Caps new undergraduate loan rates at 4%, graduate loans at 5%, and parent PLUS loans at 6%, with rates fixed for the life of each loan [S2][S3].
Eliminates origination fees on all federal direct loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2018, so borrowers receive the full amount they borrow [S2][S3].

Creates a refinancing program allowing borrowers with existing federal direct loans, and borrowers with older bank-issued federal family education loans, to move into new loans at the lower rates offered to new borrowers, with eligibility rules that prioritize borrowers with the greatest financial need [S2][S3].
Requires a public awareness campaign, run with the consumer financial regulator, to notify borrowers that they are eligible to refinance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. Lower rate caps and eliminated origination fees mean the federal government collects less interest and fee revenue on student loans, which is made up through general tax revenue or borrowing. Servicers and lenders holding older bank-issued federal loans would lose those loans when borrowers refinance them into direct federal loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and older loan holders

drawbacks.text: The lower rate caps and fee elimination reduce federal revenue from the student loan program, and that cost would fall on taxpayers generally — some of whom never attended college — unless offset elsewhere [S2][S3].

Refinancing at lower rates reduces total interest collections on the roughly $1.4 trillion federal loan portfolio, and the bill does not specify how the government would absorb that revenue loss or which other programs might be trimmed to pay for it [S3].

Refinancing older loans at lower rates, even with income-based priority rules, could deliver the largest dollar savings to borrowers carrying the biggest balances, who tend to be graduate and professional school borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the benefits are direct and substantial: lower rates on tens of thousands of dollars of debt, no fee skimmed off each loan, and a chance to refinance older, higher-rate loans. The cost is real but diffuse — it shows up as reduced federal loan program revenue spread across taxpayers, and the bill leaves the question of paying for it unanswered. The income-based eligibility rules for refinancing are a reasonable guard against the biggest savings flowing mainly to high-earning graduates, but the Secretary's rules would determine how well that works.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the bill on July 10, 2017 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student borrowers gained nothing because the bill never moved. The status quo persisted: higher loan rates, origination fees, and no refinancing option stayed in place, which preserved federal loan program revenue and the books of business of existing loan servicers and holders of older bank-issued federal loans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal loan revenue and existing servicers

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida and the bill's only sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 10, 2017 and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Higher Education Act
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 10, 2017 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 115th Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows nothing about how members of either party would have lined up.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and holders of older bank-issued federal education loans
industries.note: The refinancing program would pay off older loans held by banks and other lenders under the Federal Family Education Loan program, and newly refinanced loans would be serviced as direct federal loans. Borrowers moving out of those loans means less fee and interest revenue for the firms and lenders holding them. A fee-free, lower-rate federal loan book also squeezes the margins of companies earning revenue on servicing the current portfolio.

Lower rate caps and the end of origination fees reduce the interest and fee income the federal government collects from borrowers — in effect, the government would subsidize college borrowing more heavily out of general funds.
